--- toc-title: In this lesson --- # 12 Streamline your code In this lesson we will learn how to extract geospatial data from a CSV to create a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame`, introduce more customizations for maps and matplotlib figures, and go over strategies to streamline our code. By the end of this lesson, students will be able to: - create a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` from a CSV with longitude and latitude columns - format printed output using f-strings - use `for` loops, alone and with `zip()`, to avoid repeating code - check that their code does what they expect using `assert` - create figures with multiple axes ## About the data The U.S. energy landscape relies on a mix of fossil fuels and renewables, each with unique environmental and economic impacts. As the nation works toward sustainability and energy security, understanding this energy mix is essential for informed policy and progress toward cleaner energy. In this lesson, we will use data from the U.S. [Energy Information Administration (EIA)](https://www.eia.gov) about [operable electric generating plants in the United States by energy source, as of February 2025](https://hub.arcgis.com/datasets/fedmaps::power-plants-in-the-u-s--2/about) @eia_power_plants_2025. The dataset includes information on plant types and energy sources, offering insights into the diversity of power sources—from fossil fuels to renewables—that supply electricity nationwide. The dataset's metadata can be [accessed here](https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/b063316fac7345dba4bae96eaa813b2f/info/metadata/metadata.xml?format=default&output=html). The EIA data on electric plants has been downloaded as a CSV and reprojected into the EPSG:4269 CRS for this lesson. It can be accessed [here](https://github.com/carmengg/eds-220-book/blob/main/data/power_plants_epsg4269.csv). Each row in the data is one power plant. These are the columns we will use in this lesson, with descriptions adapted from the EIA metadata: | Column | Description | |--------|-------------| | `state` | State where the power plant is located. Also includes the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico | | `primsource` | Primary energy source of the power plant, for example solar, natural gas or wind. It is the source with the largest net summer capacity in the plant | | `install_mw` | Installed (nameplate) capacity, in megawatts (MW): the maximum output of the plant's generators as rated by the manufacturer | | `longitude`, `latitude` | Location of the power plant, in the NAD83 CRS (EPSG:4269) | Additionally, we will use a [TIGER shapefile of the US states from the United States Census Bureau](https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/tiger-line-file.2026.html#form-dropdown-790442341) @us_census_bureau_tiger_2026. [TIGER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topologically_Integrated_Geographic_Encoding_and_Referencing) stands for Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing. TIGER is the US Census Bureau's geographic database, and TIGER/Line files are extracts from it. Earlier versions of these files used a plain-text (ASCII) format; beginning with the 2007 version, they are distributed as shapefiles. You can view the metadata for all the TIGER shapefiles [here](https://www2.census.gov/geo/pdfs/maps-data/data/tiger/tgrshp2026/TGRSHP2026_TechDoc.pdf). Follow these steps to download the shapefile with the United States' states: 1. At the [2026 TIGER page](https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/tiger-line-file.2026.html#form-dropdown-790442341), under Download, click on "Web Interface" 2. For year, select 2026, and for layer type select "States (and equivalent)". Click submit. 3. Click on "Download national file". The column descriptions for the US states shapefile, from the [TIGER/Line Shapefiles technical documentation](https://www2.census.gov/geo/pdfs/maps-data/data/tiger/tgrshp2026/TGRSHP2026_TechDoc.pdf), are: | Column | Type | Description | |--------|------|-------------| | `REGION` | String | Region code | | `DIVISION` | String | Division code | | `STATEFP` | String | State FIPS code | | `STATENS` | String | State NS code | | `GEOID` | String | State identifier; state FIPS code | | `GEOIDFQ` | String | Fully qualified GEOID; used to join data tables from data.census.gov | | `STUSPS` | String | Two-character United States Postal Service (USPS) state postal abbreviation | | `NAME` | String | State name | | `LSAD` | String | LSAD code for the state | | `MTFCC` | String | MAF/TIGER Feature Class Code (G4000) | | `FUNCSTAT` | String | Functional status | | `ALAND` | Number | Land area | | `AWATER` | Number | Water area | | `INTPTLAT` | String | Latitude of the internal point | | `INTPTLON` | String | Longitude of the internal point | ## CSV to `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` Let's start by importing packages and updating viewing options: ::: {#394ee4ac .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import pandas as pd from pandas.api.types import is_string_dtype, is_numeric_dtype import geopandas as gpd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # Display all columns when looking at dataframes pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None) ``` ::: Next, we import the power plants dataset. In this lesson, we read it directly from its URL. ::: {#92eaaf30 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Import power plants data URL = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/carmengg/eds-220-book/refs/heads/main/data/power_plants_epsg4269.csv' power_plants = pd.read_csv(URL) power_plants.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The power plants file is a CSV. Unlike shapefiles or other geospatial file formats, a CSV doesn't store a geometry column or a CRS, so `geopandas` cannot reliably build them on its own. We will need to create the geometry and set the CRS ourselves. To do so we will use the longitude and latitude columns in the CSV. These indicate the location of the power plants in the NAD83 CRS (EPSG:4269). We can use this information to create a new `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` from the `pandas.DataFrame` using the `geopandas` function [`points_from_xy()`](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/docs/reference/api/geopandas.points_from_xy.html): ::: {#95e4193e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create points from latitude and longitude points = gpd.points_from_xy(power_plants['longitude'], power_plants['latitude']) # Create geodataframe power_plants = gpd.GeoDataFrame(power_plants, # Data geometry=points, # Specify geometry column crs='EPSG:4269' # Specify CRS ) ``` ::: Let's check that we now have a `geometry` column: ::: {#c4b60b2e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} power_plants.geometry ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 0 POINT (-84.29497 45.36282) 1 POINT (-83.32781 43.46590) 2 POINT (-82.93881 43.72170) 3 POINT (-85.42600 43.83930) 4 POINT (-85.85510 42.73100) ... 13440 POINT (-118.10900 34.60800) 13441 POINT (-79.28172 42.50275) 13442 POINT (-77.74272 43.18914) 13443 POINT (-75.90345 42.33782) 13444 POINT (-120.63443 37.08391) Name: geometry, Length: 13445, dtype: geometry ``` ::: ::: With the `geometry` column and CRS, we can plot our dataset: ::: {#b5a6c4b1 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} power_plants.plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-11-csv-to-geo_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=580 height=408} ::: ::: ## f-strings So far, we have printed variables by passing several arguments to the `print()` function. This means that we write commas between every string and variable we want to print, and then the `print()` function joins these into a single string, with a space between each one. For example: ::: {#abbf0cdd .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} print('CRS:', power_plants.crs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CRS: EPSG:4269 ``` ::: ::: Another popular way of mixing strings and variables in print statements is by creating an **f-string** which stands for "formatted string". The simplest syntax for an f-string is: ```python f" some text {replace}" ``` where `replace` can be a variable, an expression, or a function or method call. For example: ::: {#b21ae1bd .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Explore CRS print(f"ellipsoid: {power_plants.crs.ellipsoid}") print(f"datum: {power_plants.crs.datum}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ellipsoid: GRS 1980 datum: North American Datum 1983 ``` ::: ::: We just created a string replacing the value inside the curly brackets `{}`. One of the advantages of using f-strings is that they offer customization for formatting the output: ::: {#faccddd7 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Any expression can go inside the curly brackets # :, adds thousands separators print(f"The data has {len(power_plants):,} power plants in {power_plants['state'].nunique()} states and territories.") # :.2f rounds to 2 decimals print(f"Average installed capacity: {power_plants['install_mw'].mean():.2f} MW") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` The data has 13,445 power plants in 52 states and territories. Average installed capacity: 99.39 MW ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-caution} ## Use f-strings or not? Whether you use an f-string or simply concatenate strings with variables inside your print statements depends entirely on the application. For quickly checking a variable, a print statement might be enough, while using f-strings can be better to include custom messages during runtime. The best tool can be different depending on the task! These are some good resources to learn more about f-string formatting: - [Real Python - Python's F-String for String Interpolation and Formatting](https://realpython.com/python-f-strings/) - [Python documentation - Format Specification Mini-Language](https://docs.python.org/3/library/string.html#formatspec) ::: ## Import shapefile Let's import the TIGER shapefile ::: {#996c42f9 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Import states data fp = os.path.join('data','tl_2026_us_state','tl_2026_us_state.shp') states = gpd.read_file(fp) # Simplify column names states.columns = states.columns.str.lower() states.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: and obtain some preliminary geospatial information about the states geodataframe: ::: {#b15f762b .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(states.crs) states.plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` EPSG:4269 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-11-csv-to-geo_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-2.png){width=566 height=183} ::: ::: ## `for` loops The `region`, `division`, and `statefp` columns contain codes. The US Census Bureau groups the states into four regions (for example, the West), which are further split into nine divisions (for example, the Pacific division). Each state also has a FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code, a numeric code that identifies it. For example, California's FIPS code is 06. We will use these codes to select the states we need. It can be easier to work with the codes as numbers instead of strings, so let's update the corresponding columns in the states geodataframe. We start by checking the data type of the `region`, `division`, and `statefp` columns: ::: {#781584fc .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} code_cols = ['region', 'division', 'statefp'] # Check whether codes columns are strings for column in code_cols: print(f"{column} is string dtype? {is_string_dtype(states[column])}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` region is string dtype? True division is string dtype? True statefp is string dtype? True ``` ::: ::: Remember `for` loops execute a block of code a fixed number of times, iterating over a set of objects. In this case, we iterate over the list of column names `code_cols = ['region', 'division', 'statefp']`. :::{.callout-caution} ## DRY code We could have checked whether all the `region`, `division`, and `statefp` columns were of string data type by using the following code: ```python print(f"region is string dtype? {is_string_dtype(states['region'])}") print(f"division is string dtype? {is_string_dtype(states['division'])}") print(f"statefp is string dtype? {is_string_dtype(states['statefp'])}") ``` However, this is inconvenient as it repeats the same pieces of code, only changing the column name. Instead, using the `for` loop allows us to succinctly print the same information: ```python code_cols = ['region', 'division', 'statefp'] for column in code_cols: print(f"{column} is string dtype? {is_string_dtype(states[column])}") ``` **Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)** is a core programming principle that encourages reducing redundancy and consolidating repeated logic. Try implementing it as much as possible! If you need to repeat the "same" code more than twice, you likely need a `for` loop. ::: ## `assert` Next, we update the data type of the code columns to be integers. This time, we check the data type of the column using the `is_numeric_dtype()` function inside an **`assert`** statement: ::: {#262e2da2 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Update code columns into integers for column in code_cols: states[column] = states[column].astype('int') assert is_numeric_dtype(states[column]) # Check conversion ``` ::: The `assert` keyword does nothing if the expression next to it evaluates to `True`. If it evaluates to `False`, it raises an `AssertionError` exception and stops your code from running any further. For example, ::: {#5a424b8d .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Does nothing if statement is True assert 2+2 == 4 # Raises an error if statement is False assert 2+2 == 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

      2 assert 2+2 == 4
      4 # Raises an error if statement is False
----> 5 assert 2+2 == 3

AssertionError:
``` ::: ::: ::: In our data type conversion code, since no `AssertionError` was raised, we can be confident that the data type was updated. ## Data selection For this lesson, we want to use only the contiguous states. As seen in the plot, the data covers a bigger area. :::{.callout-tip} ## Check-in From the TIGER shapefiles metadata we know that: > In addition to the fifty states, the Census Bureau treats the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the Island Areas (American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands) as statistical equivalents of states for the purpose of data presentation. In [this US Census Bureau file](https://www2.census.gov/geo/pdfs/maps-data/maps/reference/us_regdiv.pdf) we can see what each code for the region, division, and state corresponds to. - What are the unique values for region, division, or state codes in the data? - Which codes should we select to keep only states in the contiguous US? ::: Let's go ahead and select the data: ::: {#8647f232 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Select contiguous US states contiguous = states[(states['region']!=9) & (~states['statefp'].isin([2,15]))] ``` ::: In this code we used the syntax ```python ~df['column'].isin([val1, val2, val3]) ``` The `~` tilde symbol is used in Python to negate a statement. So the previous line could be read as "the values in `df`'s column which are *not* in the list `[val1, val2, val3]`." ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check-in Select the data in the `power_plants` data frame for the contiguous US states. ::: Let's check our answer: ::: {#06779e84 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Select power plants in the contiguous US states power_plants = power_plants[~power_plants['state'].isin(['Puerto Rico','Hawaii','Alaska'])] ``` ::: ## Plotting Before we plot our data, let's make sure they are in the same CRS: ::: {#e4209c56 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} assert contiguous.crs == power_plants.crs ``` ::: ::: {#c9844336 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5)) # Update figure size # Remove the axis for a cleaner map ax.axis('off') # Title for the plot ax.set_title('Operable electric generating plants in the contiguous United States', fontsize=15) # Add states contiguous.plot(ax=ax, color='none', edgecolor='#362312') # Add electric power plants colored by energy source power_plants.plot(ax=ax, column='primsource', legend=True, markersize=4, cmap='tab20', alpha=0.5, legend_kwds={ 'title': 'Primary energy source', 'title_fontsize': 'small', 'fontsize': 'small', 'loc': 'upper left', 'bbox_to_anchor': (0, 0), 'ncols': 6 }) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-11-csv-to-geo_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=698 height=463} ::: ::: In the map above we specified the figure size when creating the plot. This size is given in inches, but [can be updated to other units](https://matplotlib.org/stable/gallery/subplots_axes_and_figures/figure_size_units.html) (pixels, cm, etc). We also controlled the legend location using `loc` and `bbox_to_anchor` in the `legend_kwds`: - `loc` indicates the corner of the legend we want to use for placement, and - `bbox_to_anchor` is a tuple with coordinates indicating where to place the corner specified in `loc` relative to the axes. Values between 0 and 1 are within the axes. `matplotlib` uses a variety of ways to locate elements within the graph and it is best to check the documentation to not spend too much time fiddling with locations. ## `for` with `zip` Often, we need to iterate simultaneously over two lists (or other iterables). The `zip()` function in Python allows you to combine two or more lists (or other iterables) so that you can iterate over their elements in pairs. When used with a `for` loop, it lets you process elements from each list together, like this example: ::: {#feb41367 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Iterate over a single list numbers = [1, 2, 3] for num in numbers: print(num) print('\n') # Blank line # Iterate over two lists in pairs using zip() letters = ['a', 'b', 'c'] for num, letter in zip(numbers, letters): print(num, letter) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 2 3 1 a 2 b 3 c ``` ::: ::: Let's see a practical application of `for` loops and `zip()` with `matplotlib` subplots. A common situation when code gets repeated is when creating subplots. For example: ::: {#6acc5dd3 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=1, ncols=3, figsize=(7, 3)) axes[0].set_title('This is axis 0') axes[1].set_title('This is axis 1') axes[2].set_title('This is axis 2') plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-11-csv-to-geo_files/figure-html/cell-20-output-1.png){width=581 height=283} ::: ::: In this example, notice that the `axes` variable returned by the `plt.subplots()` function is actually an array of axes we can iterate over. Remember that the figure and the axes are separate elements in a `matplotlib` plot. ![Image source: [Getting Started with Matplotlib](https://www.skytowner.com/explore/getting_started_with_matplotlib)](/book/images/lesson-10/matplotlib_figure_axes_axis.png) :::{.callout-tip} ## Check-in Use `for` and `zip()` to create the same subplots and avoid redundancy. ::: :::{.callout-tip} ## Exercise 1. Select the power plants in California in a variable named `ca_power_plants`. 2. Create a _list_ named `top_sources` with California's top 3 primary sources by number of power plants. That is, the 3 values of `primsource` that appear in the most California power plants. 3. Isolate the California state boundary in a variable named `ca_boundary`. 4. Recreate the following plot: ::: {#92d21370 .cell execution_count=20} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lesson-11-csv-to-geo_files/figure-html/cell-21-output-1.png){width=566 height=272} ::: ::: :::
